evaluation.positioning_hook: A recovering teen addict tries to hold her friend group together after a masked killer starts executing their darkest secrets, only to discover the murderer is one of their own.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clear horror hook: a teen friend group, a party setting, and a killer targeting hidden sins. The audience is obvious, but the script’s extreme violence and sprawling cast narrow the commercial lane rather than widening it.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The core engine is easy to explain once the killings begin: a group of teens is hunted after a shared secret trail turns into a slasher setup. The opening spends a long time on social dynamics before the threat fully crystallizes, which delays the hook a bit.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Sophia has a usable central contradiction — sarcastic, vulnerable, and trying to stay clean — and the friend group has distinct flavors. But many supporting characters are defined by one-note traits or relationship labels, so the ensemble is vivid in bursts more than durable on the page.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script is willing to go hard on melodrama, teen banter, and graphic slasher violence, which gives it some personality. But the underlying structure is familiar and the dialogue often leans on broad, repetitive teen shorthand rather than a fresh formal angle.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The party-to-killings escalation does create forward motion, and the body count keeps the page turning. Still, the first half is heavily conversational, and the repeated group-chat/social scenes slow the pressure that the horror premise needs to keep tightening.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a killer punishing a teen group for their sins is legible, but the execution lands closer to a familiar slasher framework than a truly fresh one. The reveal mechanics and revenge logic are more derivative than surprising.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The school, friend-group hierarchy, and teen social ecosystem are specific enough to feel lived in, especially through the group chat and party ritual. But the world mostly functions as a container for the killings rather than a system with deeper social rules.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a recognizable teen-horror register: crude jokes, emotional confessions, and sudden gore. The tone is consistent, but it doesn’t yet have a singular signature that separates it from the broader slasher field.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Sophia’s addiction, family trauma, and the group’s buried guilt suggest a deeper emotional engine beneath the horror setup. The script gestures at that depth, but much of it is delivered in blunt exposition rather than layered revelation.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The script is built on a web of friendships, romances, sibling bonds, and betrayals, and those relationships do generate scene energy. The best material comes from the group dynamic, even if the sheer number of characters makes some connections feel thin.

lead_characters.name: Sophia French
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 17, white or light-skinned teen, high-school student, recovering addict, emotionally volatile but resilient.
lead_characters.hook: Sophia is the script’s emotional center: sarcastic, impulsive, and visibly fragile, but trying to claw her way back from pills, self-harm, and a toxic home life. She wants to be the funny, unbothered one in the group, yet every scene keeps exposing how much she’s barely holding herself together.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young lead like Angourie Rice in The Nice Guys or Odessa A’zion in Hellraiser — a role that lets an actor play bite, shame, humor, and breakdown in the same breath. The part asks for a performer who can carry both teen charisma and raw vulnerability.

lead_characters.name: Evelyn
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16, teen sister, supportive family member.
lead_characters.hook: Evelyn is Sophia’s steadier younger sister, the one person in the house who can still reach her without a fight. She’s written as compassionate and observant, with just enough edge to feel like a real sibling rather than a saint.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded sibling role that gave Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 or Julia Butters in The Fabelmans room to be emotionally precise without carrying the whole movie. It offers an actor the chance to be the moral witness inside a chaotic story.

lead_characters.name: Bonnie
lead_characters.hook: Bonnie is the damaged parent whose apology arrives late and carries the weight of the whole family’s history. Her confession about rape and resentment gives the film one of its most loaded emotional reversals, even if the scene is bluntly written.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of heavy, confession-driven maternal role that can give an actor the same kind of bruised showcase as Patricia Clarkson in Pieces of April or Toni Collette in Hereditary. It’s a scene-part with real awards-adjacent emotional material.

lead_characters.name: Maddy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 18, senior, group leader, aspiring performer/businesswoman.
lead_characters.hook: Maddy reads like the social center of the friend group: older, protective, ambitious, and carrying her own guilt from a fatal hit-and-run. She has the strongest “leader of the pack” energy in the ensemble and the clearest off-ramp into a bigger life.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of layered teen-leader role that can do for an actor what Maude Apatow got in Euphoria or what Rachel Zegler got in The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes — charisma, authority, and a hidden fracture line. It gives a performer a chance to play confidence that’s already cracking.

lead_characters.name: Nate
lead_characters.demographics: Male, teen, bi, recently bereaved, athletic build.
lead_characters.hook: Nate is the quiet, emotionally sealed friend whose grief and family trauma make him feel like the group’s most withdrawn presence. He’s written as mysterious and self-contained, which gives him a useful contrast against the louder characters around him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of restrained, grief-saturated teen role that can showcase the same inward pressure as Justice Smith in The Get Down or Harris Dickinson in Beach Rats. It gives an actor a chance to play silence as active behavior.

lead_characters.name: Sam
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16, goth-presenting teen, introverted, queer-coded or bi-coded through dialogue context.
lead_characters.hook: Sam is the dry, history-loving outsider inside the friend group, and the script uses her as both comic friction and moral counterweight. She’s one of the few characters whose interests and voice feel specific rather than interchangeable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp, off-center teen role that can give an actor the same scene-stealing lane as Jenna Ortega in Scream or Auli’i Cravalho in Crush. It offers a chance to play deadpan intelligence with emotional loyalty underneath.

lead_characters.name: Emma
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16, teen, twin sister to Sam.
lead_characters.hook: Emma is the more openly romantic, impulsive twin, and the script uses her as a contrast to Sam’s cooler exterior. She’s emotionally reactive, jealous, and blunt, which makes her useful in scenes that need friction fast.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of volatile teen supporting role that can pop the way a performance in Bodies Bodies Bodies or Euphoria does — fast, messy, and highly playable. It gives an actor a chance to swing from flirtation to rage in one scene.

lead_characters.name: Bryan
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 16, teen boyfriend, polished and self-regarding.
lead_characters.hook: Bryan is the polished boyfriend with a romantic pose and a messy private life, which makes him a built-in source of betrayal. He’s more interesting as a pressure point in the ensemble than as a standalone engine, but he does carry real jealousy and guilt.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of conflicted teen male role that can give an actor the same slippery appeal as a character in Cruel Summer or The Summer I Turned Pretty. It’s a chance to play charm, cowardice, and romantic self-justification.

lead_characters.name: Kyle
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 16, teen boyfriend, later revealed as killer.
lead_characters.hook: Kyle starts as the supportive, affectionate boyfriend and ends as the film’s most load-bearing betrayal. The reveal that he’s one of the killers gives the role a clean genre turn, even if the character’s psychology is more declared than dramatized.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of reveal-role that can give an actor the same late-game switch as a slasher villain in Scream or Fear Street. The showcase is the pivot from soft-boy intimacy to cold, ideological menace.

lead_characters.name: Nancy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 17, loyal friend, socially central teen.
lead_characters.hook: Nancy is the dependable organizer type, the friend who keeps trying to hold the group together even as the night collapses around her. She has enough warmth and social authority to feel like a real anchor in the ensemble.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of ensemble-support role that lets an actor play competence under pressure, similar to a grounded teen role in Yellowjackets or Scream. It gives the performer a chance to be the emotional logistics manager of the group.

lead_characters.name: Phoebe
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 17, teen friend, sincere and honest.
lead_characters.hook: Phoebe is one of the more straightforwardly kind members of the group, which makes her useful as a moral barometer. She doesn’t get as much depth as Sophia or Maddy, but she helps keep the ensemble from becoming all snark all the time.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sincere supporting role that can give an actor the same clean, sympathetic lane as a friend character in a teen ensemble film. It’s a good part for someone who can play warmth without disappearing.

lead_characters.name: Tina
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 17, teen new girl, snarky and self-contained.
lead_characters.hook: Tina is the blunt, sexually aggressive comic disruptor in the group, and she’s written to say the thing everyone else won’t. She’s abrasive enough to be memorable, even when the dialogue pushes her into broadness.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp-edged supporting role that can give an actor the same scene-chewing freedom as a teen in Bottoms or Bodies Bodies Bodies. It’s a showcase for timing, attitude, and controlled chaos.

lead_characters.name: Jade
lead_characters.hook: Jade is the friend whose departure and death become a major emotional trigger for the group, and she’s written with enough social sparkle to feel like a real loss. Her final scenes also make her the story’s most explicit victim of the killer’s moral crusade.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of short-but-pivotal role that can give an actor a memorable emotional imprint, similar to a key victim role in a slasher franchise. It’s a chance to make a strong impression fast.

lead_characters.name: Zoey
lead_characters.hook: Zoey is a late-arriving supporting character whose panic, pregnancy reveal, and death add another layer of dread to the school storyline. She’s less developed than the core group, but she broadens the film’s sense of collateral damage.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of brief but intense supporting role that can give an actor a high-impact horror sequence. It’s a pure survival-and-fear showcase.

lead_characters.name: Nate
lead_characters.demographics: Male, teen, bi, recently bereaved, athletic build.
lead_characters.hook: Nate is the quiet, emotionally sealed friend whose grief and family trauma make him feel like the group’s most withdrawn presence. He’s written as mysterious and self-contained, which gives him a useful contrast against the louder characters around him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of restrained, grief-saturated teen role that can showcase the same inward pressure as Justice Smith in The Get Down or Harris Dickinson in Beach Rats. It gives an actor a chance to play silence as active behavior.

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical gore and a few TV/camera feed moments; no major effects worldbuilding.
technical.sfx_needs: Heavy practical blood effects, stabbing effects, decapitation and body-damage makeup, police break-in beats.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best suited to streaming-first or specialty theatrical horror distribution.

budget.note: Contemporary locations keep the base spend contained, but the amusement park, diner, multiple houses, night exteriors, and repeated practical gore sequences add up quickly.

casting.note: The film needs a large teen ensemble that can all read as distinct, plus a lead who can carry addiction, family trauma, and final-girl pressure. The killer reveal also depends on the audience buying Kyle as both boyfriend and threat.

development.note: The script’s emotional material is broad and often stated outright, and the killer’s moral logic is tied to a long chain of confessions and flashbacks. That makes the page-to-screen calibration a real development conversation.

comp_set.title: Scream
comp_set.why_it_comps: Teen ensemble slasher energy, self-aware horror banter, and a killer reveal inside a friend-group ecosystem.

comp_set.title: Fear Street Part One: 1994
comp_set.why_it_comps: Group-based horror with teen relationships, escalating body count, and a streaming-friendly gore-forward lane.

comp_set.title: Bodies Bodies Bodies
comp_set.why_it_comps: Young ensemble dynamics, social friction, and a murder-mystery pressure cooker built around a party.

comp_set.title: I Know What You Did Last Summer
comp_set.why_it_comps: Teen guilt, hidden wrongdoing, and a slasher engine that punishes a social circle for a buried past event.

audience_target.primary_audience: Teen and young-adult horror audiences who want a friend-group slasher with relationship drama and a heavy body-count payoff.
audience_target.demographics: Primarily 16-34, female-skewing but with male horror crossover; strongest with streaming-first genre viewers.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary teen horror with a large cast, practical gore, and a handful of contained locations keeps it in indie feature territory.

types_of_buyers: indie financier looking for elevated teen horror
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the teen-horror lane where relationship drama and kill-set pieces are the selling points. The ensemble and explicit violence make it a fit for buyers who want a high-concept, youth-facing genre play rather than a prestige drama.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The killer reveal resolves the central engine, and no side character is developed enough to justify a clean spinoff vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Sophia has a real final-girl contradiction.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the movie a lead role with actual casting value: a teen who can be funny, damaged, defensive, and emotionally exposed in the same scene. Buyers can see a performer-driven horror vehicle rather than just a body-count exercise.
strengths.evidence: Sophia’s pill-bottle bathroom scene, her rehab confession at the diner, and her sarcastic group-chat voice all point to the same fractured center.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The friend group has usable social texture.
strengths.what_it_means: The ensemble gives the script a built-in audience hook because the horror is attached to recognizable teen dynamics: couples, best friends, siblings, jealousy, and old loyalties. That makes the movie easier to market than a faceless slasher.
strengths.evidence: The group-chat banter, the amusement park outing, the diner table, and the party fallout all build a social web before the killings begin.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The killer’s moral crusade is a clean genre engine.
strengths.what_it_means: A punishment-based slasher premise is easy to pitch, easy to trailer, and easy for a buyer to understand in one sentence. The sins-and-consequences framing gives the film a built-in hook for marketing and audience curiosity.
strengths.evidence: The letter naming the next targets and the repeated “bad people deserve punishment” logic drive the reveal structure.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Practical horror is the production sweet spot.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie can deliver a lot of screen value through makeup, blood, and performance rather than expensive VFX, which is attractive to indie horror buyers. That keeps the project in a financeable lane while still promising audience-pleasing set pieces.
strengths.evidence: The kills are built around bathrooms, sheds, windows, and house interiors rather than effects-heavy environments.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The sibling bond gives the film heart.
strengths.what_it_means: Sophia and Evelyn create a second emotional lane that can widen the audience beyond pure horror fans. That kind of family anchor helps a genre movie feel less disposable and gives the lead a human stake outside the romance web.
strengths.evidence: Their car scenes, mutual protectiveness, and the repeated emphasis on being “unstoppable” together.

whats_special.headline: This is a teen slasher with a real lead role at its center and a marketable punishment engine around it. The combination of a damaged final girl, a social-media-era friend group, and practical gore keeps it in a buyer-friendly indie horror lane that can be sold on cast and premise.

items.detail: The script keeps stacking confessions, flashbacks, and ideological speeches to justify the murders, especially once Parker and Kyle are revealed. That makes the reveal feel more narrated than discovered, which is a real pressure point for a slasher buy.

items.area: The opening runs long before the threat lands.
items.detail: The first act spends a lot of time on group-chat banter, outfit descriptions, and social dynamics before the horror engine fully takes over. For a feature in this lane, that delays the genre promise buyers expect to see early.

The Jade/Tori sequence and later kill scenes are written with graphic sexualized mutilation and prolonged body damage. That narrows the buyer pool and pushes the project toward a harder mature-content lane than a broad streamer horror play.

items.area: The ensemble is large but unevenly defined.
items.detail: Sophia, Maddy, Sam, Nate, and a few others have distinct energy, but several supporting players are mostly one-note relationship functions. That creates a casting and audience-recognition issue because not every name in the group feels equally load-bearing.

A lot of scenes circle the same emotional beats — friendship, loyalty, trauma, who likes whom — without much escalation in subtext. That can flatten momentum and make the script feel longer than the premise needs.

issues.headline: The biggest friction is that the script explains its villainy more than it dramatizes it, which undercuts the mystery and makes the reveal feel over-argued. Add the very explicit violence and a large ensemble with uneven definition, and this becomes a buyer conversation about execution as much as premise.
